text.L1: Fractions are numbers, so they have places on a number line.
text.L2: The bottom number tells how many equal gaps to make from 0 to 1.
text.L3: Count gaps, not marks. Four marks between 0 and 1 make five equal gaps.
text.L4: So each gap is one fifth. The top number tells how many gaps to count from 0.
text.L5: To mark two fifths, count two gaps from 0. That mark is 2/5.
text.L6: A fraction can also go beyond 1. If the top number is bigger than the bottom number, it lies past 1.
text.L7: For example, 5/4 is one quarter past 1, so it is after 1.
text.L8: Now use these ideas to choose where 5/4 belongs.

text.L7: Even plus even is even, while odd plus even stays odd because one leftover remains.

text.L1: Water is found in three forms: liquid, solid ice, and invisible water vapour.
text.L2: Liquid water is in seas, rivers, lakes and under the ground. Solid water is ice, snow and glaciers.
text.L3: Water vapour is a gas in the air, and we cannot see it.
text.L4: Water changes form, but it is never destroyed. A puddle dries when its water evaporates into the air.
text.L5: Later, vapour can cool and condense into drops. Water can also freeze into ice and melt again.
text.L6: About 97 out of every 100 parts of Earth's water is salty sea water, so most water cannot be drunk.
text.L7: Most fresh water is frozen or underground. Less than one part in 100 is in rivers, lakes and reachable ground water.
text.L8: Because usable fresh water is shared by everyone, we must not waste or dirty it.

els.text: A wrong prediction wastes the test

text.L1: Science is not just a list of facts to memorise. It is a way of finding out by observing, asking questions and testing ideas.
text.L2: Start by noticing something. Ask a question that you can answer by doing something and observing or measuring what happens.
text.L3: Before the test, make a prediction. It is a guess with a reason, based on what you already know.
text.L4: For example, ask whether curd sets faster in a warm place or a cool place. Predict that the warm bowl will set first because the starter bacteria work faster in warmth.
text.L5: Test fairly with the same milk, the same amount and the same starter. Keep one bowl warm and one bowl cool, then observe and record them after the same time.
text.L6: The result may support the prediction or may not. A wrong prediction is still useful because it teaches us something new and leads to another question.
text.L7: Remember the circle: observe, ask, predict, test and conclude. Then use what you learned to ask a new question.

text.L1: A change can be physical or chemical. The key question is: has a new substance formed?
text.L2: In a physical change, shape, size or state changes, but no new substance forms.
text.L3: Melting ghee is physical. It is still ghee, and it becomes solid again when cooled.
text.L4: Dissolving is also physical. Sugar spreads into water, but it is still there and still has mass.
text.L5: In a chemical change, one or more new substances with different properties are formed.
text.L6: Gas bubbles, a colour change, heat or light, a new smell, or a new solid can be evidence.
text.L7: Here is a common myth: dissolved sugar has disappeared and has no mass. Not true; dissolving does not make the sugar vanish.
text.L8: Baking soda and lemon juice fizz because a new gas forms. That is a chemical change.
